questions.q: Your business can switch everything off for the whole copy. Which cutover approach fits best?
options: Phased, one group at a time
Big bang, copy it all in one go
Trickle, a little at a time
Replication-based, with changes kept in sync
questions.explain: Big bang copies everything in one operation, then switches. MongoDB says it is faster but needs downtime, so it fits a system that can be offline for the whole copy and whose data is small enough.

questions.q: What does Google's architecture guide say about moving a database with zero downtime for clients?
options: It is easy with the right tool
It only works for small databases
It needs a storage device shipped to you
It is impossible, so near-zero is the real goal
questions.explain: Google's guide says truly zero downtime for clients is impossible. Near-zero is the goal, because there is always a short pause.

questions.q: In a near-zero downtime move, why is there still a short pause?
options: Writes stop briefly so the last changes can catch up
The old system must be deleted first
All the data is copied for the first time
Users need time to learn the new system
questions.explain: That pause is the draining step. Writes stop on the source while the last changes are applied. That drain, plus switchover testing, is why you get near-zero instead of zero.

questions.q: Why is comparing row counts not enough to prove a migration worked?
options: Counts take too long to run
Counts catch missing rows, but not a value that quietly changed
Counts only work on tiny tables
Counts are not allowed on live data
questions.explain: Counts catch missing rows. They won't catch a changed value, so save a stronger check for the tables that matter most, like money or customer records.

questions.q: After you switch to the new system, why can going back to the old one lose recent work?
options: The old system is always deleted at switchover
Backups stop working after a switch
New writes land on the new system, so the old one goes stale
Clients keep writing to both systems after the switch
questions.explain: After switchover the source stops receiving changes. Google's fallback phase copies target changes back to it, so a reverse move stays possible.
